revisits.item: Hikers who reach the bare summit ridge often assume a fire stripped it, but no fire was needed: ten thousand years of wind and frost have worked a slow (i) ___, carrying the soil downhill grain by grain until only the granite was left. That granite is now the sole (ii) ___ on which the orange lichens grow, and they draw nothing from it but a place to hold on. The gray jays that haunt the summit cairn are often called pests, but the word overstates the case; their tie to the hikers is merely (iii) ___, a matter of living off dropped crumbs that no hiker misses. · blank 1: precession / denudation / speciation; blank 2: locus / hinterland / substrate; blank 3: commensal / maladaptive / conspecific
revisits.change: new sentence logic: a contrast instead of a cause, or a concession instead of a restatement

revisits.item: Rather than courting (i) ___, the poet sets clotted consonants against her long vowels, so that each line's harshness acts as a (ii) ___ to its sweetness rather than a flaw in it. Her reasoning, given in a late essay, is that unbroken sweetness does not delight the ear for long but comes to (iii) ___ it, lulling the reader into hearing sound without sense. · blank 1: tranquillity / jargon / euphony; blank 2: welter / counterpoint / equivocation; blank 3: stultify / champion / tender
revisits.change: new format: an SE item becomes a TC blank, or a TC blank becomes an SE pair

revisits.item: Purists accused the translator of having (i) ___ the epic, mixing in idioms of her own century until its ancient voice was hard to hear; her defenders replied that the literal versions had left the poem in so (ii) ___ a state, unread outside a few seminars, that only a bolder rendering could have saved it. · blank 1: adulterate / enhance / attenuate; blank 2: remedial / covert / parlous
revisits.change: a different SE partner or a different sense of the word

revisits.item: The old grammarian's (i) ___ that no sentence may end with a preposition was repeated for a century by teachers who never asked where it came from. Its most zealous (ii) ___ was a newspaper style editor who rewrote reporters' copy to obey it, however strained the result. Ironically, the reporters' mocking compliance, which buried prepositions in ever more tortured clauses, did more to (iii) ___ the rule than any linguist's critique: readers who had never questioned it began to find it ridiculous. · blank 1: jeremiad / rodomontade / dictum; blank 2: hedonist / apostle / boor; blank 3: second / subvert / saturate
